content.title: #Skyking (2026) ⭐ 7.4 | Documentary, Thriller
content.text: Videos1Photos1Featured reviewsAn unexpectedly beautiful filmI remember the story when it happened and I watched this documentary last night on Hulu. It was not what I expected. Surprisingly heartfelt story of a broken man who did something he shouldn't have done but for whom you can't help but identify with on so many levels. Great documentaries have the ability to take quick blurb viral news stories like this one was and drill deeper to find the human story at the core. That's exactly what this film did and I was surprised how emotional it got. Where I was expecting a "look how crazy this was" dry run through of what happened, it was so much more than that.I'll also note a lot of the 1 star reviews on here really missed the point, to the level where I don't think many of them watched the film but instead just responded to the surface level news story. Yes, what he did was dangerous, but the film isn't attempting to excuse or justify that. What it's doing is giving context to someone with a troubled past and exploring the variables that pushed him past his breaking point. Regardless of how you feel about what he did, you could not possibly watch this film and not find Russell to be an incredibly sympathic & relatable character.RIP Sky KingLike many others, I stumbled across the viral ATC recording a few years ago on social media - the voice of Richard 'Beebo' Russell, calmly talking as he flew that stolen plane over Seattle. And like so many people, his story hit me deeply.It bypassed the analytical part of my brain and went straight to something human.There was something raw in his voice. Polite. Self-aware. Almost apologetic. You could hear intelligence, humor, even kindness. And beneath all of it - pain. There's a moment in his voice where you can tell he wishes someone had stopped him earlier in life, not that day. Beebo did not sound hateful, enraged, or chaotic. He didn't want to hurt anyone. That dissonance is what unsettled so many people. It challenges our assumptions about crisis and despair. It raises uncomfortable questions about how suffering can remain invisible, especially in individuals who appear functional and composed. How pain can coexist with normalcy - and how easily it can go unnoticed.That raw material is powerful on its own.Which is why #Skyking, directed by Patricia E. Gillespie, feels surprisingly flat.The documentary's strongest contribution is access. Hearing from Richard's family, who remained private for years, adds essential human context and grounds the story beyond headlines. It reminds the viewer that this was not just an aviation incident, but a personal unraveling with real people left behind.But structurally, something feels off.The storytelling lacks momentum and psychological depth. It moves chronologically without building real insight. It presents information rather than interpreting it. For a story that sparked such a profound emotional response worldwide, the film feels oddly subdued.The emotional weight comes not from the filmmaking, but from the original audio itself - which remains more powerful than the film built around it.As a documentary, it's so-so on a good day.As a human story, it's far more powerful.The takeaway isn't about aviation security or viral infamy. It's about paying more attention to the people around us. The ones who don't demand attention. The quiet ones. The funny ones. The polite ones. The ones who never want to bother anyone.They are often the ones carrying the heaviest pain.RIP Sky King.Not a documentary - it's an excuse for bad behavior.This film is a sickening romanticization of the life of a psychologically imbalance man, who placed the lives of many innocent people in peril. And, by his selfish and criminal behavior, caused the professionals who had to deal with his actions significant emotional trauma that will haunt them for the rest of their lives.The incessant placing of blame for his actions on the company, his bosses and the flight crews is shameful. There was no justification for what Richard Russell did. It wasn't his inability to promote. It wasn't his race. It wasn't the low pay and long hours. It was his own narcissistic desires to prove he deserved more. Blame-placing, emotional reasoning, overgeneralization and mental filtering are just a few of the classic Thinking Errors demonstrated.I remember watching this incident as it happened and thinking it was somewhat tragic. Watching this documentary, however, had me wishing they had shot him down.The Story Behind the HeadlinesI went into #SKYKING knowing nothing and ended up watching a story that goes far beyond the headlines. What starts as an unbelievable event becomes something much more human through the use of real air traffic control audio and deeply personal interviews.Instead of focusing on spectacle, the film challenges how quickly people label and simplify complex situations. It asks you to sit with discomfort rather than giving easy answers, especially when it comes to mental health.What stayed with me most is not just what happened, but how quickly people decided they understood it. This is a thoughtful documentary that looks past the noise and asks you to do the same.A note on how this film was madeAs someone connected to this story, I want to share some context that isn't in the film.The family contributed personal home footage to this production. They received no compensation from what became a commercially distributed theatrical release( a thriller, smh). Early conversations included suggestions of donating a portion of proceeds to a nonprofit - that has not materialized. They are now being asked to participate in a publicity/ impact campaign on the film's behalf.The film elevates individuals whose real lives don't reflect how they're portrayed - because they fit a narrative the director had already decided to tell.I don't question anyone's right to make a film. I do think audiences and industry professionals deserve to know that the people closest to this story did not share in its commercial success, and that some commitments made during production remain unfulfilled.I'll let that speak for itself.More like thisRelated interestsA troubled airport worker's impulsive decision to steal and fly a commercial plane becomes a gripping aerial drama that reflects deeper issues of mental health and working-class struggles in America.Plot summaryAdd synopsisEverything New on Hulu and Disney+ in AprilEverything New on Hulu and Disney+ in AprilFreshen up your Watchlist with the latest roster of streaming movies and TV shows coming to Hulu and Disney+, featuring old favorites and top-notch newcomers.See the listContribute to this pageSuggest an edit or add missing contentEdit page
